stops.name: Bems by the Korka, City of Löver
stops.campa: The empire the boy-emperors carved apart at Verdun this year has left Bertane inside Lothair's middle kingdom, and Arthur's court, wintering now more often than not from Karidoel, keeps long seasons at Bems, the city Wolfram sets by the little river Korka in the land he calls Löver: Beaune, on the Burgundian plain. Years turn over here while Gawain wanders, his forty-day trial grown into a longer quest, and while Parzival, cursed and silent, seeks Munsalvaesche alone. Arthur waits, as a king must, holding the middle of the story while its edges range far from him.

stops.name: The Messenger from Gawain Reaches Bems
stops.campa: A footman reaches Bems from the Rhine with a letter that bears no seal and needs none. Gawain has broken a bough from King Gramoflanz's tree, and Gramoflanz, who stood unarmed and would not fight one man alone, named the terms himself once the names were out: the sixteenth day, at Ioflanz on the plain, and Arthur may come up from Bems by the Korka in eight days. So Gawain asks his uncle for the whole court as witness, and for the one man whose word can end a blood-feud too old to remember its own cause. Arthur sends the herald back in two days with his promise.
stops.quote: At Château Merveil; and on thy side thine uncle can others bring, from the land that he rules, King Arthur, and Löver its name shall be, and the city is Bems by the Korka... There lieth he now with his vassals, and hither can make his way, in eight days, with great joy; so I bid thee to meet me... at Ioflanz upon the plain.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIII, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), King Gramoflanz naming the day to Gawain

stops.name: Arthur Breaks Camp at Beaune
stops.campa: At dawn the second day after the herald's word, Arthur's household rides out of Bems in full array: Guinevere and her ladies among the columns, the great round silk on its wagon, knights of a dozen lands who have wintered at his court. The road runs east from the Burgundian plain toward the young mountains and the great river, five days of ordinary marching set against the vast distances the poem elsewhere claims for such journeys, because Bems and Ioflanze, on the ground Greub actually walks, lie closer to one another than the singer's rounder eight days would have it.

stops.name: Past Logrois in the Sundgau
stops.campa: On the third day the column passes within sight of Logrois, the fortress the poem gives to the duchess Orgeluse, which Greub sets on this ground at Landser in the Sundgau. The poem follows Arthur nowhere along this road and gives the march no incident; only the castle stands here, and it stands as the quarrel's own source. Orgeluse's love was killed by Gramoflanz, and her grief hired every knight who ever rode for her, Gawain among them. Arthur rides past the walls of the wrong that he is going to the Rhine to unmake, and the poem does not say whether he looks up at them.

stops.name: The Rhine Plain at Kembs, the Sixth of May
stops.campa: On the sixth day Arthur's column comes down onto the flat water-meadows of the Rhine north of Basle, the plain Wolfram calls Ioflanze, and finds Gawain's camp and Gramoflanz's already pitched over against one another, hosts a mile and more in length with the ladies' bridles ringing among them. Trumpets sound the king's arrival; Gawain rides out bareheaded to meet him, and Guinevere is welcomed by Queen Arnive, Gawain's own grandmother, found alive after Klingsor's long enchantment. Two armies gathered for a duel of honor become, in a single afternoon, one great encampment waiting to see whether it ends in war or a wedding.

stops.name: The Hosts Assembled
stops.campa: For two days the plain at Joflanze fills further: Klingsor's freed queens ride in from Chastel Marveil, Orgeluse's knights make camp beside Arthur's, and heralds go between the tents arranging precedence and truce. Arthur sends his own messengers to Gramoflanz to plead the Table's honor for Gawain, and is refused; the king will keep the day he swore. So Arthur weighs the old wrong that started the feud and works the other way instead, as he worked it on the Birs six years before, to see whether a king's word can settle what private killing cannot. It is the same discipline, tested now on two armies.

stops.name: Gawain and Parzival, Unknowing, at Arms
stops.campa: On the morning the Gramoflanz duel should be fought, Gawain rides early to the ground and finds a stranger there in unmarked armor. They joust on the dewy grass, both go down with their horses, and they fight on with swords until the shields are hewn to splinters and the hours run out. It is Parzival, and he has the better of it: Gawain is near beaten when Arthur's returning pages cry his name across the field. The stranger throws his weapon from his hand and weeps that his luckless hand has fought so sinful a strife. Gawain, unhelmed, tells him plainly the victory is his.
stops.quote: Alas! that with gallant Gawain I have foughten so fierce a fight, 'tis myself whom I here have vanquished, and my joy shall have taken flight... For thy kinsman am I, and cousin, and men call me Parzival!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Gramoflanz Reconciled, Arthur's Peace
stops.campa: Arthur takes the quarrel out of the field entirely. With Brandelidelein of Punturtois, Gramoflanz's own uncle, he divides the work: Brandelidelein will bring his nephew round, Arthur will bring the Duchess. He rises from the feast, walks out to Gawain's tent, carries the terms back, and by the day's end has turned a duel to the death into a wedding. Orgeluse gives Gramoflanz the kiss of forgiveness for her slain love, weeping as she gives it; Gramoflanz and Gawain kiss and end the strife; and Arthur gives Itonje, Gawain's sister, to the king to wife, generous as ever with gifts that cost him nothing and restore everything.
stops.quote: Then Arthur the wise and courteous, he brought the tale again, and King Gramoflanz, for his garland, henceforward must mourn in vain... Then Gramoflanz and Sir Gawain with a kiss put an end to strife; and Arthur gave maid Itonjé to King Gramoflanz to wife.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Feirefiss, the Brother Both Black and White
stops.campa: A magnificent unknown knight lands from ships on the Rhine and rides into camp in armor sewn with jewels, seeking adventure; Parzival meets him at arms before either learns the other's name, and the fight goes hard until Parzival's sword shatters on the stranger's helm. The heathen could kill him now and says so, then will not: he flings his own blade away into the wood so the contest stands even. Only then does he ask what face Parzival's brother bears. Parzival answers on Ekuba's word, black and white as written parchment, and the heathen says: then that brother am I. They unhelm and embrace as kin.
stops.quote: Quoth Feirefis, 'Now, thou hero, by thy courteous breeding fair, since in sooth thou shalt have a brother, say, what face doth that brother bear?'... Quoth the Waleis, 'As written parchment, both black and white is he, for so hath Ekuba told me.' 'Then that brother am I alway,' quoth the heathen... hatred and wrath were slain here in a brotherly embrace.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Cundrie's Second Coming, the Grail Crown
stops.campa: On Whitsun Saturday, six years to the season since she cursed him on the Birs, Cundrie the sorceress rides again into Arthur's camp, but kneels now before Parzival instead: the throne of the Grail has passed to him, she says, and Anfortas may at last be released from his long wound if Parzival will come and ask the question he once failed to ask. Arthur's whole court hears the reversal of that old shame. Parzival, Feirefiss and Cundrie ride out from Joflanze together toward Munsalvaesche, and the king's part in the story, though not the story itself, draws toward its close.

stops.name: Dianazdrun, the Court Comes Home
stops.campa: Whitsunday crowns Parzival at Munsalvaesche and the great camp on the Rhine empties, every company taking the road it knows. Arthur turns his household back into the heart of Bertane, a week of ordinary marching down the Saône valley on the old Roman roads, away from the frontier and its enchantments. The court that has spent this whole story as a camp, a lodge, a riverside pavilion, comes at last to a city: Dianazdrun, the place later ages will call Dijon, seat of the dukes who will one day rule this same Burgundian land the poem has been quietly describing all along under other, older names.

stops.name: Schamilot, the Round Table's Last Seat
stops.campa: Arthur comes at last to Schamilot, the seat by Dianazdrun that Weston renders with the only Camelot this whole poem contains: a low rise of ground outside Dijon where, five centuries hence, Duke Philip the Bold will raise the Chartreuse de Champmol as the necropolis of Burgundy's own dukes, and set Claus Sluter's mourning figures to weep in stone around it. The poem does not know that future and does not need to; it only sets the Round Table down here, at journey's end, on the ground that will keep faith with it, in its own fashion, for as long as Burgundy remembers its dead.
stops.quote: King Arthur to Camelot journeyed with many a hero true.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894); Weston notes this as the poem's only mention of Camelot, identified by Werner Greub with Champmol, Dijon
